title: Starbirth with a chance of winds?
caption: The galaxy NGC 4861, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 4861 · constellation Canes Venatici · about 30 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: This galaxy looks rather like a comet, with a dense, luminous, colorful head and a dimmer tail trailing behind. It is NGC 4861, in the lesser-known constellation Canes Venatici, the Hunting Dogs.
Astronomers are still debating how to classify it. Its physical properties, such as mass, size and rotation speed, point to a spiral galaxy, but its appearance fits better with a dwarf irregular.

Small, messy galaxies like this are useful to study. Their gravity is weaker, so it takes less energy to move material around inside them. That makes them likely to be filled with galactic winds, fast streams of charged particles. Star formation can power such winds, and new stars are forming in NGC 4861's bright head, blasting out high-speed particles. It would seem an ideal place to study galactic winds, yet recent studies found none.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.24 x 2.59 arcminutes) and distance (30 million light years), the frame spans roughly 28,000 × 23,000 light-years. Its light set out about 30 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared data from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys with filters from Wide Field Camera 3 that isolate glowing sulfur and nitrogen. The color assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The galaxy is far too faint to see by eye, and part of the data is near-infrared light that the eye cannot detect.
